title: The npm Worm That Shipped With a Valid Sigstore Badge: Mini Shai-Hulud, Explained
description:
Last week, a worm hit forty two npm packages in six minutes. Every one of them shipped with a valid Sigstore attestation. The green provenance badge said it was safe.
 
That's Mini Shai-Hulud. The May 11, 2026 TanStack incident, which spread to 170+ packages across npm and PyPI.
 
Npm provenance was supposed to make this impossible. Trusted Publishing signs each release with a short-lived OIDC token. The badge proves the pipeline built the file.
 
Here's the chain. The attacker forked a TanStack repo and opened a pull request. A pull_request_target trigger ran the fork's code on the trusted runner, poisoning the build cache. When a maintainer later merged a real PR, the release workflow restored the poisoned cache and scraped the live OIDC token straight out of /proc/PID/mem. The worm republished itself to npm with a real Sigstore signature. No credentials stolen. No 2FA prompt. Valid provenance generated on the fly.
 
The honest limit: SLSA Level 3 attestation only proves which pipeline built the artifact. It does not prove the pipeline was honest. Two different questions. Provenance answers the first. It does not answer the second.
 
The fix is OIDC scope. Pin Trusted Publishing to one workflow file on one protected branch, and never check out fork code on pull_request_target. Don't rotate tokens before isolating the host either, because the worm has a gh-token-monitor daemon that wipes the disk if it detects revocation.
 
Provenance proved the pipeline. The pipeline lied.
 
Sources: socket.dev, stepsecurity.io, wiz.io, openai.com.
